items.readable_text:
Content:
How can we calculate [MATH: \displaystyle{\int} \sin x \cos x \, \textrm{d}x?]

Content:
Notice that we have the product of sine and cosine with the same argument [MATH: (x).] In such cases, we can use the double-angle formula for sine to solve the integral.

Content:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for sine, which is
[MATH: \sin {2x}=2\sin x \cos x.]
We can rearrange the above formula as
[MATH: \sin x \cos x = \dfrac{1}{2} \sin {2x}.]

Content:
Plugging this into our integral, we get

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\int \sin x \cos x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \dfrac{1}{2}\sin {2x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
&=\dfrac{1}{2} \int \sin {2x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
&=\dfrac{1}{2} \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} \cos {2x}\right )+C \[5pt]
&=-\dfrac{1}{4} \cos {2x}+C.
}]

Content:
In general, we can use the double-angle formula for sine to solve any integral that's of the form

Content:
[MATH: \int \sin\left(ax+b\right)\cos(ax+b)\,\textrm{d}x.]

Content:

sections.normalized_html: Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle{{\int}} \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2} \right)\cos \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\, \textrm{d}x.]
sections.readable_text: Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle{{\int}} \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2} \right)\cos \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\, \textrm{d}x.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

[MATH: \sin {2\theta} =2\sin \theta \cos \theta\quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\theta) = \sin{\theta}\cos{\theta}.]

Letting [MATH: \theta= \dfrac{x}{2},] we get [MATH: \eqalign{ \dfrac{1}{2} \sin \left(2\cdot \dfrac{x}{2} \right) &= \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2} \right)\cos\left( \dfrac{x}{2}\right)\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{2}\sin x &= \sin \left( \dfrac{x}{2}\right) \cos \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right). }]

Therefore,

[MATH: \eqalign{ \int \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \cos \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \dfrac{1}{2}\sin {x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2} \int \sin {x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2} \left( - \cos {x}\right )+C \[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{2} \cos {x}+C. }]

Letting [MATH: \theta= \dfrac{x}{2},] we get

\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x	&= \sin \left( \dfrac{x}{2}\right) \cos \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right).

&=\dfrac{1}{2} \int \sin {x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
&=\dfrac{1}{2} \left( - \cos {x}\right )+C \[5pt]
&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \cos {x}+C.
}]

sections.normalized_html:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the [MATH: \cos^2{x}] term, given by

[MATH: \cos{2x} =2\cos^2 x -1.]

Rearranging, we have

[MATH: \cos^2 x = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\cos 2x +1 \right).]

Substituting this into our integral, we get

[MATH: \eqalign{ \int \cos^2 x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\cos 2x +1 \right) \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int ( \cos {2x} +1) \textrm{d}x\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin {2x} +x\right) + C\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4}\sin {2x} +\dfrac{1}{2}x + C. }]
